prize_parts.citation: for the discovery of gamma-ray burst afterglows, which established the cosmological origin of gamma-ray bursts

statement.case_for: I keep B025 as my preferred single-part prize. Having read the whole first round, it remains the only shortlisted entry where nature handed us a result that no one expected and that has stood unchanged for nearly three decades: gamma-ray bursts are extragalactic, extremely luminous, and tied to the deaths of massive stars and to neutron-star mergers. The chain is short and decisive. BeppoSAX gave arcminute X-ray positions within hours, which made the afterglow, host-galaxy and redshift observations possible, and those observations ended a thirty-year argument. Thousands of afterglows, supernova associations and the 2017 merger event have only reinforced it, so there is no maturity question of the kind that hangs over B021, B020 or the source astronomy in B052. The credit also divides along a real line: the instrument and localisation (Costa, Frontera) and the follow-up that identified the counterparts and established distance (Kulkarni). That tells us something about how stars die and what the early universe looked like, which is the sort of discovery I think the prize exists for.
statement.case_against: The credit is open to challenge and I do not want to hide that. The optical afterglow and first redshift came from ground-based groups, and van Paradijs (deceased) and others such as Groot cannot be named, so a three-name list is a simplification of a team effort. Kulkarni's name represents radio and optical follow-up and redshift work more than the first optical detection, which means the citation must be worded around afterglows and the cosmological origin and not around one detector. Only Pearce ranked it besides me, so I am clearly not speaking for a committee majority, and others may regard it as astronomy at the edge of the physics remit. Finally, three names use the whole budget, so it can only stand as a single-part prize.

responses.point: Pearce ranks B025 second, keeps it as first alternative, and worries that the optical-identification credit (van Paradijs, Groot) is more open than the BeppoSAX instrument credit, and that three names exhaust the budget.
responses.response: This is the right worry, and I answer it by being narrow about what the citation claims. The prize would be for the afterglows and the cosmological origin, not for the first optical photon. The decisive step was localisation fast enough to let anyone point a telescope at the right place, then radio and optical follow-up that fixed distance and energy scale. Costa and Frontera own the first, and Kulkarni, through the radio afterglow and redshift programme, owns a large part of the second, even though van Paradijs would also have deserved recognition. I accept that this leaves a gap, but a gap of that kind exists in almost every prize built on an observational campaign. I also agree that B025 does not combine with another part, so we should treat it as a single prize, and I do not see that as a defect.

responses.point: Kroll treats lattice clocks (B024) as a stand-alone prize whose value is a new measurement capability, with the reservation that this is close to the 2005 and 2012 prizes and that priority has not been checked.
responses.response: I take the argument that a new capability can be the achievement, and I rank clocks well enough to list them as an alternative. But Kroll himself concedes that the output so far is tighter limits, not a new fact about nature, and that the redefinition of the second has not happened. A prize now would reward an instrument that is still waiting for its own payoff. If clock comparisons had produced a drift in constants or a dark-matter signal, I would move at once. As it stands, I regard the clean Katori-Ye credit as the best feature of B024 and the nearness to Hall, Hansch and Wineland as a real cost, so I place it behind a result that nature has already delivered.

responses.point: Eriksson holds that B021 is robust because many groups reproduced the correlated phases, and that Bistritzer should be kept because the 2011 prediction is a two-author result; he would accept the pair as a fallback.
responses.response: Eriksson's argument about the theory slot persuades me on credit: a prediction by Bistritzer and MacDonald is misdescribed if only MacDonald is named, so I now think three names is the more honest B021 list, and I withdraw my earlier preference for dropping Bistritzer. My remaining difference is timing. The flat-band mechanism is understood, but the superconducting pairing is not, and the field is eight years old. That is why B021 is my first alternative and not my first choice. If the committee wants a condensed-matter prize this year, I would vote for it with all three names and without any reluctance about the discovery itself.

responses.point: Lindroth prefers B020 with Bloch, Greiner and Zoller, saying the Mott transition and single-site observation were themselves the discovery, while admitting the doped Hubbard payoff is still absent and that any trio leaves out strong contributors.
responses.response: I find Lindroth's reading of the Mott transition as a result in its own right fair, and I agree it is a clean experiment. But her own case against shows why I hesitate: five credited names, an unsettled split between Zoller and Esslinger, Cirac and Zoller shared with B006, and a headline payoff that is still in the future. That is a lot of unresolved attribution for a prize meant to be obvious once the work is done. I would rank B020 below B025 for that reason, though I recognise it is mature as a technique and would not object strongly if it were the committee's choice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts three names that cover the BeppoSAX localisation and the radio and optical follow-up, given that van Paradijs is deceased and Groot and others cannot be named.
Whether colleagues will count gamma-ray burst astronomy as physics for this prize, since only Pearce ranked it besides me.
Whether the committee can settle on a credible set of names for IceCube within three people, because I would then reconsider it for a later year.
Whether the pairing mechanism in twisted bilayer graphene will be understood soon enough that B021 becomes the better choice.
statement.conflict_note: No conflict or recusal to disclose. None of the credited people on the shortlist are among my known connections (Gross, Rubinstein, Van Riet, the Uppsala string group), and my own work on string theory and dark bubble cosmology does not touch these entries. I note that as Secretary I know the procedure, but that does not give me any stake in a particular outcome.
